summary:
Visitors stand under the national framework in every state. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying an X remain valid until they expire. Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. A civil-liberties union has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Oklahoma restricts facility use by statute. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker lists Oklahoma under K-12 school-facility bans, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025, grouping it with the states that bar transgender people from bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity. Nationally, such bans are in force in nine states and one territory, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

Birth certificates are the live document question in Oklahoma. House Bill 1225, which would require a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibit changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to Governor Kevin Stitt's desk as of 6 May 2026. Its authors say it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including Tulsa resident Rowan Fowler, and the state Attorney General's office confirmed the bill clarifies that Oklahoma never permitted gender birth-certificate changes; critics called it further discrimination.

The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map assigns Oklahoma its per-state grade and lists the state among the worst for legislation targeting transgender adults. That edition added a fourth 'Do Not Travel' state and tracked changes to the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier.
tangentialFactors:
Foreign governments have responded to the federal document rules publicly. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Internal risk gradings have hardened. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Facility enforcement is no longer theoretical. In April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Document restriction is being copied across state lines. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, and rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. Oklahoma's House Bill 1225 is presented by its authors as reinforcing a statute already under federal challenge rather than as a new restriction.

Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no ban on trans facility use, so the rules a visitor encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

House Bill 1225 would fix birth certificates to a male or female designation and prohibit changes with very little exception. As of 6 May 2026 it had passed 70-17 and was awaiting Governor Kevin Stitt's signature. outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Governor Kevin Stitt signed House Bill 1225 is unresolved in the sources: the available local coverage is dated 6 May 2026 and describes the bill as having reached the governor's desk, with no later status reported.

Oklahoma's specific letter grade on the July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map is not stated in the sources; only that the assessment assigns the state a grade and lists it among the worst for legislation targeting transgender adults.

Whether Oklahoma appears in the assessment's 'Worst Laws Passed' tier is not sourced. The inventory records only that the July 2026 edition tracked changes to that tier.

The outcome of the federal challenge to Oklahoma's birth-certificate law, and the effect House Bill 1225 would have on that litigation, are not sourced.

Oklahoma's rules for changing gender markers on driver's licences are not sourced here. The Movement Advancement Project maintains a state-by-state identity-document map covering licence and birth-certificate marker changes, but the Oklahoma entry itself is not reproduced in the inventory.
